title: Low-Level Decision Order
explain: When a system is too slow or too big, I reach for mechanisms in order of increasing complexity. First eliminate unnecessary work, then replicate capacity, then partition stateful parts, and use a queue when arrival time and processing time do not match. Each step adds operational cost, so I pay for it only when the cheaper step is exhausted.
model:
Core principle: the lower the complexity, the earlier it comes.

```
1. Eliminate work      cache, dedup (single-flight), batch
2. Replicate capacity  more stateless instances; then ask WHY you cannot keep replicating
3. Partition state     stateful node is the limit -> partitioning / sharding
4. Absorb mismatch     work arrives at a different rate/time than it is processed -> queue
```

- Step 1 adds almost nothing: work not done costs nothing. Example: 10,000 rows/s written at 2 ms per call plus 0.01 ms per row costs about 20,100 ms of database time per second unbatched, but batching 100 per call costs 100 calls x 3 ms = 300 ms.
- Step 2 hits a wall at anything stateful, such as one database primary; that wall tells you what to partition ([sharding](#/sd/f/sharding)).
- Step 4 smooths bursts; it does not fix sustained overload, because the backlog just grows.

It is a heuristic: a queue can be the simplest first fix for a bursty, delay-tolerant workload. Use [high-level thinking](#/sd/f/high-level-thinking) to learn which bottleneck you really have.

details.q: Why does the order put eliminate-work before add-instances before shard?
details.a: Each step adds more operational complexity: removing work adds almost nothing, replicating stateless instances adds routing, sharding adds rebalancing and cross-shard operations. Pay for the cheaper fix first and move down only when you can explain why it no longer helps.

details.q: A report API recomputes the same aggregation and 40% of requests are exact repeats; CPU is saturated. What first?
details.a: Cache or single-flight identical computations. Removing 40% of the work is cheaper than any structural change; more instances would also work but pay for the redundant computation forever.

details.q: A stateless tier has 40 instances but p99 is bad, and the single Postgres primary is IOPS-saturated around the clock. Next step?
details.a: Partition or shard so writes spread over several primaries. You have hit the step-2 wall: the bottleneck is stateful. A queue only smooths bursts and a read cache does not reduce writes.

details.q: Traffic spikes tenfold for five minutes every hour and a few minutes of delay is fine. What fits?
details.a: A queue between producers and workers: the issue is arrival time versus processing time and delay is acceptable. Provisioning for peak wastes capacity most of the time, and sharding fixes volume, not burstiness.

details.q: When is a queue not the answer?
details.a: When load is sustained above capacity, since the backlog grows without bound, or when callers need an immediate answer. Then you need less work, more capacity or partitioning.

details.q: Show a numeric example of eliminating work by batching.
details.a: 10,000 rows/s with 2 ms per call + 0.01 ms per row: one row per call costs 10,000 x 2.01 = 20,100 ms/s, about twenty cores. Batches of 100 give 100 calls/s x 3 ms = 300 ms/s. Batching removed per-call overhead.

prompts.q: State the low-level decision order and the reason for it.
points: Eliminate work, replicate, partition state, queue
Each step has a cost you pay only when needed
It is a heuristic, not a law

prompts.q: A service is slow. Walk through how you would diagnose and pick a fix using this order.
points: Find the bottleneck first (CPU, stateful store, bursts)
Check for repeated or batchable work
Scale stateless tier and see why it stops helping
Use a queue for burst or timing mismatch

prompts.q: Distinguish when to choose a queue versus sharding.
points: Sharding: sustained volume beyond one stateful node
Queue backlog grows if overload is sustained
Sharding does not smooth bursts by itself
